#620. The EPA’s Chemical-Detecting Plane Isn’t Doing Its Job Anymore

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2423 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

The EPA’s Chemical-Detecting Plane Isn’t Doing Its Job Anymore

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2423 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When an ammonia leak outside a hotel in Weatherford, Oklahoma, injured 74 people last November, the federal government's chemical-detection plane stayed on the ground.
  • When a fire tore through a Valero refinery in Port Arthur, Texas, in March, the plane sat idle.
  • And when massive blasts killed two workers at an industrial recycling plant in Toledo, Ohio, in August, it stayed put, despite a fire surrounding tanks of flammable solvents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When an ammonia leak outside a hotel in Weatherford, Oklahoma, injured 74 people last November, the federal government's chemical-detection plane stayed on the ground.

When a fire tore through a Valero refinery in Port Arthur, Texas, in March, the plane sat idle.

And when massive blasts killed two workers at an industrial recycling plant in Toledo, Ohio, in August, it stayed put, despite a fire surrounding tanks of flammable solvents.

“Ten years ago, it would have gone to all of them,” notes Mark Thomas, a former EPA official who for years managed the airborne detection effort.

The program, known as ASPECT, was designed to respond around the clock to emergencies involving toxic chemicals, oil spills, and radiation. The plane’s sensors could identify chemicals in the air within minutes, giving emergency responders crucial information about the dangers nearby communities face.

For more than two decades, the plane has flown over many of the country’s worst disasters, from Fresh Orleans after Hurricane Katrina to the deadly West Fertilizer explosion in Texas to the Deepwater Horizon oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico.

But since early 2021, the single-engine Cessna has responded to just seven emergencies. And former ASPECT scientists say two of those missions—the 2023 train derailment that sent toxic clouds over East Palestine, Ohio, and the 2025 fire at Smitty’s Supply in Louisiana—were badly mismanaged.

It has been revealed that at Smitty’s, the EPA declared the air safe, but a former ASPECT scientist later found toxic chemicals the agency had missed. And the agency’s inspector general is now auditing the response to the East Palestine derailment, including the data behind its public assurances about air quality.

According to recent reports, in June, the EPA inspector general found a more fundamental problem: The plane could no longer identify chemicals within minutes, as designed. Instead, the data had to be analyzed by hand, a process that takes about a week. That’s far too long to help anyone on the ground who’s deciding whether to evacuate.

The EPA said the plane's chemical sensors are wearing out and expects replacements to be working by mid-2027.

It has been revealed that but five people who helped build and run the program told Floodlight that the EPA is fixing the wrong problem. The old sensors still work, they say. What the agency lost, in their view, is the initiative and expertise that made the program a powerful tool when disaster struck. Replacing the old sensors, they warn, could leave the EPA even less capable of detecting hazardous chemicals in an emergency.

According to recent reports, “I fear that the public is at risk,” says Robert Kroutil, a longtime ASPECT scientist who helped develop the program and later became a whistleblower. “It’s such an key program, and they've allowed it to waste away to nothing.”.

The EPA did not respond to Floodlight’s requests for an interview or questions about ASPECT’s decline, its handling of emergencies, the replacement of its sensors, and allegations of mismanagement by former program scientists and managers.

The country’s need for a chemical-sensing plane grew from the smoldering, toxic debris in Manhattan on September 11, 2001, when the EPA’s monitoring trucks were stranded on the wrong side of the Hudson River, unable to cross after bridges and tunnels into the city closed.

Kroutil was a program manager for the Department of Defense at the time, leading a research team that had developed the technology that would become ASPECT, short for Airborne Spectral Photometric Environmental Collection Technology.

The military transferred the program to the EPA for use in detecting hazardous chemicals during civilian emergencies.

It became a critical tool for emergency responders over the next 20 years.

For 72 hours after Hurricane Katrina struck, it was the only emergency response aircraft flying over New Orleans, where it helped locate a missing 55-gallon drum of potentially lethal chloroacetic acid.

During the Deepwater Horizon disaster, it became a key tool for tracking oil slicks in the Gulf of Mexico.

And when a fire engulfed 15 massive tanks at a chemical storage terminal east of Houston in 2019, the ASPECT plane helped emergency responders track the plume, which contained the carcinogen benzene.

Richard Lawhorn, an assistant chief with Harris County’s hazardous materials response team in Texas, claims the plane could detect chemicals at elevations beyond the reach of ground crews and survey a much wider area in a short time. Unlike ground monitors, the plane can scan a swath of air three-quarters of a mile wide, capturing a far broader picture of potential hazards.

“They’re monitoring the products we can’t reach,” he notes.

The program’s success lay in its intellectual rigor: Kroutil and the program’s radiological lead held PhDs, as did Mark Thomas, the former EPA official. The team wrote the code, designed the mounts that held gear, and analyzed the raw data themselves.

“We were very, very hands-on and intimately familiar with every part of that aircraft,” states Thomas, who later went to work for a firm that develops chemical-sensing technology.

The decline began with the departures of key ASPECT personnel during President Donald Trump’s first administration.

As part of an agency reorganization, the EPA told the program’s staff in 2019 that they had to relocate to Texas, where the plane was based, or face termination, documents show.

The mandate was unnecessary, according to Thomas, because the program had been designed for remote operation. Rather than leave his elderly parents in Kansas, he retired. Then, ASPECT’s radiological lead left the division, and the engineer who helped build and manage the plane’s sensors accepted a demotion to stay in Kansas.

According to Kroutil and two of his former colleagues, the EPA then failed to fill those vacancies with scientists who had any experience with airborne chemical detection.

“They lost the institutional knowledge of the program, and quite frankly, lost the momentum of the program,” Thomas indicates.

Industry observers note that during its first two decades, the plane flew almost 80 emergency missions—an average of roughly four a year. In the past five years, however, it has flown an average of just one a year.

In October, hundreds were evacuated—and more than 50 were treated at hospitals—when a 5,500-gallon industrial tank in Toledo, Ohio, leaked glycidyl methacrylate, a chemical used in making plastics that is a probable carcinogen suspected of causing genetic defects. It was one of at least 80 chemical emergencies this year that the plane did not respond to.

The decline comes as accidental chemical releases are becoming more common. The US Chemical Safety Board tracked 133 last year, up from 83 in 2021.

The Trump administration, meanwhile, has proposed rolling back federal safeguards designed to prevent chemical disasters, including requirements for some plants to undergo independent safety audits and provide hazard information to nearby communities.

It has been revealed that former ASPECT program managers say they used to actively track chemical emergencies and urge EPA on-scene coordinators—who manage environmental emergencies—to deploy the plane. After they left, that proactive approach vanished: The plane stayed in a Texas hangar until coordinators requested it, they say.

Scott Smith, an independent environmental tester who’s often called on by local communities to investigate chemical contamination after industrial accidents, claims ASPECT could help him target his soil and water testing by mapping the path of chemical plumes. Deployed regularly, he says, the plane could save lives. Instead, “it's being shut down and not used.”.

On February 3, 2023, a Norfolk Southern freight train carrying the carcinogen vinyl chloride and other hazardous chemicals derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, near the Pennsylvania border.

As fires from the derailment smoldered, emergency responders feared an explosion—and made the controversial decision to vent and burn five railcars containing vinyl chloride, sending a towering plume over the town.

ASPECT missed the vent-and-burn operation, and its services weren’t requested until more than two days after the initial disaster. Even then, it was used sparingly. Despite the derailment being one of the nation’s worst chemical disasters in years, Kroutil claims, the plane collected just eight minutes of chemical data when it finally flew over East Palestine on February 7—a fraction of what it typically gathered during an emergency.

Had the plane been deployed earlier—or flown over the site en route to Pittsburgh, the nearest major airport—its thermal detection equipment might have helped determine that the tank cars were not in danger of exploding, Kroutil later noted in an affidavit.

Sources indicate that the National Transportation Safety Board concluded that the vent-and-burn operation had been unnecessary. It found no evidence of the dangerous chemical reaction that Norfolk Southern and its contractors said threatened an explosion. Temperature readings indicated the railcars were cooling.

According to recent reports, an EPA inspector general investigation later found a series of errors in the East Palestine response: The agency had poorly documented its procedures and failed to adequately inform emergency responders of the plane’s capabilities. The on-scene coordinator, who didn’t request the plane until two days after the derailment, wrongly believed that ground-level monitoring would provide better data.

Sources indicate that frustrated by how EPA officials were running the program, Kroutil retired. Two of his colleagues also left, further draining the program’s pool of experience and expertise.

On August 22, 2025, a massive explosion ripped through Smitty’s Supply, a facility that blended and packaged oil and other engine lubricants in Roseland, Louisiana.

Sources indicate that less than 4 miles away, Ronnie Polezcek and his family heard something hitting their roof that afternoon. At first, they thought it was raindrops.

But when they walked outside, Polezcek says, “It was just like it was raining oil.”.

The dark residue covered the family’s 23-acre farm. Polezcek says he had to burn his hay, move his cows temporarily to Mississippi, and replace a metal roof that could not be scrubbed clean. Two of his cows miscarried soon afterward, he says, and a veterinarian found arsenic in one of them. Polezcek filed a lawsuit against Smitty’s in September 2025 that has been consolidated into an ongoing class-action case.

The Smitty’s fire burned for nearly two weeks, sending a huge plume of smoke into the air. Local authorities ordered a 1-mile evacuation around the plant, and the EPA dispatched ASPECT—the plane’s first emergency deployment in 19 months.

The agency didn’t publicly post findings from the ASPECT flights until August 31, nine days after the fire began. Those reports show the air around Smitty’s contained ozone and three other pollutants but at levels far below those considered harmful to human health.

A later analysis of the raw flight data, though, told a very different story.

Sources indicate that working with the Government Accountability Project, a nonprofit that advocates for whistleblowers, Kroutil obtained data from ASPECT’s third flight over the disaster area. He indicates it took him weeks to analyze it, doing by hand what the plane’s software was designed to do in minutes.

It has been revealed that kroutil identified high concentrations of the neurotoxicant toluene and the carcinogens trichloroethylene and naphthalene, among other toxic chemicals. He concluded that the levels of toluene were so high, they could have put nearby communities at risk.

Many of the findings also matched what Smith, the independent environmental tester, detected in soil and water after the fire.

The EPA later acknowledged a similar problem, according to records that the Government Accountability Project obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request.

In a May 2026 email, an EPA manager said some target chemicals might have been present in data from the third flight but weren't flagged at the time the data was collected. The manager suggested that deterioration of the aging sensors might have contributed to the failure.

Polezcek believes officials should have evacuated a larger area.

“I really think it was a pitiful job,” he says. “They just kept saying, ‘There’s nothing to worry about, you’re good to go.’”.

In June, the EPA inspector general confirmed that Kroutil’s warnings were justified: The plane could no longer provide chemical-monitoring data within five minutes.

Recent findings suggest that instead, scientists had to conduct manual analysis that would take about a week. The EPA also failed to tell on-scene coordinators that the program isn’t working as designed.

According to recent reports, EPA officials blamed the delays on old sensors. The agency bypassed competitive bidding to award a Canadian company, Telops, a $1.7 million contract for replacement sensors designed for several applications, including gas detection and mineral mapping. Integrating the new sensors won’t be complete until “early to mid 2027,” according to the EPA.

Recent findings suggest that in contract documents, the EPA cited peer-reviewed studies showing the Telops sensors had been field-tested and proven. But much of the research on the new equipment has focused on tracking methane leaks, not the wide range of toxic chemicals released during complex industrial emergencies.

Five people formerly involved with ASPECT have raised concerns that the fresh sensors will be less capable than the old ones at detecting hazardous chemicals during industrial emergencies.

Exosens, the parent organization of Telops, told Floodlight that its system and the old one use “different measurement architectures.”.

The upcoming sensors, it notes, can identify hundreds of chemicals and distinguish chemical plumes from surrounding objects. The original infrared sensors, built by the Canadian firm Bomem, were rebuilt multiple times and equipped with new software.

In a recent development, chris Manning, an infrared spectrometer expert with no ties to Telops, the EPA, or the firm where Thomas now works, states the latest Telops sensors could complement ASPECT’s older sensors but would be a poor replacement. They are slower, less sensitive, and less suited to moving targets, he says.

“To say, ‘We're just going to replace these other two instruments’ … I mean, that’s ludicrous,” he states.

The old sensors had problems, too. Their artificial intelligence software had not been retrained after an electrical malfunction several years ago, Kroutil and Thomas say. In early 2023, contract scientists with the program presented the EPA with a proposal to retrain the software, emails show. But the EPA never took the required steps, according to Kroutil and Rick Turville, a former ASPECT manager who left the program in 2025.

Kroutil and his former colleagues say they have no confidence that the fresh sensors will fix the problem. They expect the program to deteriorate further.

In the affidavit submitted to the Government Accountability Project, Kroutil offers a dim prognosis: “Unless major changes are made at EPA and with the ASPECT program, it is not going to get any better and EPA will be flying blind.”.

#619. US tightens AI chip export controls to deter Chinese companies from accessing compute remotely

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (756 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

US tightens AI chip export controls to deter Chinese companies from accessing compute remotely

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (756 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the Trump administration on Monday is preparing to roll out fresh export controls on AI chips and data centers outside the U.S., seeking to prevent companies, especially those in China, from getting past U.S.
  • Under the interim rule, the Commerce Department will require companies to get licenses to export, reexport, or transfer AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere in the world if they may provide compute to companies in China or other restricted countries.
  • The remote-access rules target companies based in the U.S.’s D:5 group of embargoed countries, which includes China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and 18 others.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Trump administration on Monday is preparing to roll out fresh export controls on AI chips and data centers outside the U.S., seeking to prevent companies, especially those in China, from getting past U.S. export controls by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries.

Under the interim rule, the Commerce Department will require companies to get licenses to export, reexport, or transfer AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere in the world if they may provide compute to companies in China or other restricted countries.

The remote-access rules target companies based in the U.S.’s D:5 group of embargoed countries, which includes China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and 18 others.

According to recent reports, the U.S. already has rules requiring chip companies to get a license to ship AI chips to companies based in, or owned by any business in, this group of countries.

“This latest control is a logical extension of existing controls,” the interim rule reads. “These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models.”.

Recent findings suggest that the move comes days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned amid a scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy linked to one of the chipmaker’s customers. The U.S. government has reportedly been wanting to put that customer, Megaspeed, on a special entity list, as it believes the company has been buying thousands of Nvidia chips to provide compute to Chinese businesses to get past existing export-control restrictions.

Reuters reported last week that Chinese AI companies are rushing to secure computing capacity overseas amid fears of tighter restrictions from the U.S.

The rule applies to data centers or any network that can supply over 12 million total processing performance (TPP), an export-control metric the U.S. uses to measure computing power. (Twelve million TPP roughly works out to the max computing power of about 750 Nvidia H100 or H200 chips.) The rule also covers indirect access through go-betweens or brokers, and exporters and data center operators are required to keep an eye on their customers’ ownership structures and activities to ensure they aren’t run by anyone from the D:5 group.

It has been revealed that the rule also adds newly introduced licensing requirements for chip exports, reexports, or transfer of advanced semiconductors to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil. The Commerce Department noted it had included these as they “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.” For these countries, however, the license requirements will not apply to chips “destined” for companies based in the U.S.

Existing data center operators providing services that fall under this upcoming rule are required to get licenses within 90 days of the rule coming into effect.

Notably, the rule doesn’t apply to commercial recommendation systems, like those used in e-commerce or social media.

The rule also rescinds the Biden admin’s AI Diffusion Rule from January 2025, which sought to impose country-level limits on exports of advanced AI chips, and restrict transfers of certain powerful AI models. That May, the Trump administration stated it would throw out that framework, arguing that it added unnecessary restrictions on U.S. companies and the country’s allies.

Industry observers note that “By making these changes, this IFR prevents the use of certain SI items in data centers and at a computing power level that can be used for training or running of advanced SI models,” the rule reads. “Access to such computing power can be used to train and run advanced SI models capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten U.S. national security or foreign policy interests.”.

Apple releases beta 2 for iPadOS 27.3, watchOS 27.3, and more

  • In a recent development, apple has just released beta 2 for iPadOS 27.3, watchOS 27.3, visionOS 27.3, and more.
  • Two weeks ago Apple introduced an exciting wave of beta updates as iOS 27.3 and companion releases introduced many newly introduced features.
  • Siri AI upgrades are a big focus in 27.3, with upcoming languages, Siri Recap, and advanced in-app actions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, apple has just released beta 2 for iPadOS 27.3, watchOS 27.3, visionOS 27.3, and more. It’s available for developers, but a public beta will likely follow in the next couple days.

Two weeks ago Apple introduced an exciting wave of beta updates as iOS 27.3 and companion releases introduced many newly introduced features.

Siri AI upgrades are a big focus in 27.3, with upcoming languages, Siri Recap, and advanced in-app actions. There’s also a preview of new third-party app capabilities for Siri.

Industry observers note that the all-new Health app has returned in iOS and iPadOS 27.3, this time with the expectation of launching in the public release. Fitness also adds a new Gym Strength program.

Apple Music now has a Selfie Sing feature for creating personal karaoke videos, and an improved lyrics view. Safari adds Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode, and more.

According to recent reports, that’s just a sampling of the latest features in beta 1. And now today, beta 2 is here for iPadOS 27.3, watchOS 27.3, visionOS 27.3, and more.

Sources indicate that we’re expecting to see additional new features and refinements today, like video podcasts being added to the Apple TV app. We’ll keep you posted on everything noteworthy we discover.

watchOS 27.3 has one of my personal favorite fresh features in Siri Recap, so I’m curious to see if Apple keeps refining the experience throughout the beta in response to user feedback.

In a recent development, have you found anything new in beta 2 for iPadOS 27.3 or another update? Let us know in the comments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Martinis are flowing from the chimneys at Pinewood Studios, which can only mean one thing: We have our latest James Bond.

On Nov. 16, Amazon MGM Studios declared that the newest 007 will be Robert Pattinson. He takes over the role from Daniel Craig, whose last film was 2021's No Time to Die. The next Bond film, the franchise's 26th, will be helmed by Dune director Denis Villeneuve. Pattinson has also worked with Villeneuve on Dune: Part Three.

Aside from the Bond announcement, 2026 has been a banner year for Pattinson. He topped the box office with The Odyssey and cemented himself as an A24 darling with roles in The Drama and Primetime.

Industry observers note that while Pattinson has starred in smaller, stranger indie projects, he has also developed a seemingly paradoxical reputation as a franchise man. He is Batman, after all, with The Batman: Part II set for a Feb. 18, 2028 release. Before Pattinson became Battinson, moody eyeshadow and all, he captured hearts as Edward Cullen in the Twilight franchise, as well as Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter.

Plus, while not part of a franchise, his role as agent Neil in Christopher Nolan's Tenet proved he's got the chops to play a suave agent.

Other contenders for film's most famous spy included Slow Horses' Jack Lowden, One Night Only's Callum Turner, Challengers' Josh O'Connor, and Superman's Nicholas Hoult, all of whom reportedly screen tested for the role. Frankenstein's Jacob Elordi and Sinners' Jack O'Connell were reportedly in the running as well, although did not end up screen testing. Audible turns to AI to help owners discover audiobooks

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (593 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that amazon-owned audiobook service Audible is turning to AI to help listeners find their next book.
  • The overview audio itself is generated using AI, and the commentary is pulled from recordings of past Audible interviews, the company notes.
  • The idea is that this type of expanded introduction to a story could help customers decide what to listen to next, particularly when they’re on the go and don’t have time to scroll through comments or reviews.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that amazon-owned audiobook service Audible is turning to AI to help listeners find their next book. The firm on Monday rolled out a newly introduced “audio discovery” feature that provides a brief overview of a book’s themes and a summary of what readers liked about it, as well as commentary from an Audible editor or an author, in addition to playing the narrated sample.

The overview audio itself is generated using AI, and the commentary is pulled from recordings of past Audible interviews, the company notes.

The idea is that this type of expanded introduction to a story could help customers decide what to listen to next, particularly when they’re on the go and don’t have time to scroll through comments or reviews.

In a recent development, the feature follows last month’s launch of a handful of AI tools that let owners engage more with the story, interact with characters, or catch up with the help of recaps. These features have come as Audible faces newly introduced competition in the audiobooks market, namely from Spotify, which introduced audiobook listening hours as part of its paid subscriptions. That service expanded last month to over 180 markets.

According to recent reports, audible’s newly introduced feature takes a cue from how Amazon is already using AI to help people shop: On the Amazon storefront, AI can summarize buyers’ product reviews so shoppers can get a quick sense of what people had to say, as well as the pros and cons of a particular item. In Audible’s case, it’s pulling information about what people liked about the book from publicly available reviews.

It has been revealed that but such a feature could limit owners’ exposure to negative reviews if the AI only pulls information from those that offer positive remarks. (Further testing will be needed to see if this is the case, of course.).

Audible notes the overviews will also draw on other publicly available materials, like synopses and metadata.

The feature will initially be available for select English-language titles in the U.S., and will arrive alongside upcoming personalized collections based on users’ listening taste that could help them find other books.

The company’s other recent AI features, Recaps and the interactive “Ask a Question” tool, are also now expanding to more U.S. titles, and will become more broadly available in December. These features will only be available to customers who have purchased a title or who have access to the book as part of their Audible membership, the company mentioned.

“Picking your next listen should feel like getting a tip from a friend,” remarked Andy Tsao, Audible’s chief product and analytics officer, in a statement. “With audio discovery, you’ll get a quick audio take on why the title might be right for you from our editors, fellow listeners, or even the author. Some of the best listening experiences are those rare finds or hidden gems, and we want to make those great discoveries happen more often and more easily,” he added.
